description: We are a group of high school students passionate about integrating biotechnology, computational biology, software engineering, ethical AI, and entrepreneurship to address real-world challenges in healthcare and business. With experience in wet-lab techniques, biological research, data analysis, and coding, we aim to develop innovative applications, research platforms, and physical tools that bridge scientific discovery and technology to create meaningful, practical solutions.
summary:
Vitalis is an astronaut health dashboard built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. It gives crew members and flight surgeons a single, fully offline tool that turns daily check-ins (sleep, mood, nutrition, exercise, cabin CO2, fluid intake, EVA activity, symptoms) into a personal in-flight baseline, flagging deviations before they become problems, backed by real physiology.
Built in are 12 evidence-based mission-medicine checks grounded in NASA and peer-reviewed research: space anemia, cabin CO2/headache risk, kidney-stone risk, space adaptation syndrome, an orthostatic-intolerance stand test, spacewalk injury tracking, career radiation dose against the 600 mSv limit, exercise logged by device (ARED/T2/CEVIS), medication expiry, mid-mission morale drift, family/psych support logging, and a 45-day return-to-gravity reconditioning tracker. A keyword-based “Ask the doc” assistant answers common medical questions offline, with an AI assistant when network access is available.
It matters because long-duration spaceflight causes physiological decline such as bone loss, fluid shifts, radiation exposure, and muscle atrophy that’s hard to track by memory or paper logs, especially with communication delays to ground control. Vitalis puts continuous, personalized monitoring directly in the crew’s hands.
details:
Vitalis is for long missions where the crew has to handle things on their own because messages to Earth take hours. It sets up a personal baseline for each astronaut that changes slowly over time using their own readings for blood pressure, heart rate, sleep, and the rest. That baseline helps separate normal ups and downs from something that actually needs attention.

The detection part looks at several indicators at once instead of one at a time. It catches combinations that might not stand out alone, like a slight temperature rise with bad sleep and higher stress. Alerts come with some explanation of what shifted and how sure the system is. There is also a simulator that shows how the whole thing keeps running when the link to Earth is down for a while.

The main goal seems to be cutting down on false alerts so people keep trusting it. In the tests, it picked up real changes earlier than the fixed threshold version or the single indicator one. It was built in JavaScript and React with custom code for the statistics side no libraries, just the math written out and checked with test scripts.

What stands out is the built-in validation setup with synthetic missions that have known answers and the three systems compared directly. It also shows where the approach still misses things like slow drift in one reading. Real mission issues like data gaps and sensor noise were kept in mind, along with not letting the software ever give medical advice or claim more than it can prove.
